evidence.quote: Were you approached by community and/or political party representatives?

claims.text: The stem asks whether representatives approached 'you' during the interview visit, but the literal 'you' does not fix respondent versus interviewer; the item records an approach report, not the respondent's own partisan attachment and not whether anyone actually influenced answers.

evidence.quote: Did you feel threatened during the interview?

claims.text: Records a felt-threat yes/no report during this specific interview, an affective report whose addressee is not fixed by the literal 'you' rather than a respondent trait or a verified security incident.

evidence.quote: Were you physically threatened during the interview?

claims.text: Separately asked and separately coded yes/no report of physical threat during the interview; it is not nested within Q106D and co-occurrence across the pair is unobserved, so no complementary pattern or non-contradiction reading is asserted.

The three-point scale records the interviewer's attributed assessment of the respondent's candor during the encounter, a demeanour judgment rather than a validated accuracy check; only three labels appear with no special response codes, so missing and response handling is undetermined.

evidence.quote: must always obey the laws and the courts

claims.text: Forced choice between presidential exemption from law and courts and obligatory obedience, capturing a stated general constitutional stance rather than a verdict on any named ruling or observed executive conduct.

evidence.quote: armed forces should never intervene in the country's political process

claims.text: Elicits a general norm about military non-intervention in politics, set against a conditional takeover claim, so it registers a stance on the abstract design rather than approval of any concrete coup or event.
Asks the respondent to allocate oversight responsibility normatively, naming a should-be overseer for elected MPs rather than reporting whether any overseer actually acted.

Repeats the normative oversight-allocation question for the presidency with a shared option set, letting the office vary while the response act stays fixed, so differences are readable only within those offered categories.

evidence.quote: she will be criticized, called names, or harassed

claims.text: Respondent estimates the likelihood that a hypothetical woman candidate would face community sanction, an anticipated social reaction about a possible candidacy rather than a report of harassment experienced.

evidence.quote: should government and elected officials be doing more

claims.text: Records an evaluative demand about the desired direction and amount of state effort on women's rights, so a more-request is a claim about what ought to be done rather than evidence that current effort is deficient in fact.

evidence.quote: which of the following issues related to women's rights and equality

claims.text: Single-choice priority among an offered issue list, yielding a capped top pick whose option set bounds what can be named rather than independent salience ratings for each concern.

evidence.quote: using the police and security forces to enforce public health mandates

claims.text: Agreement is solicited about a possible emergency policing power as conditionally justified, so a high answer endorses a hypothetical temporary measure rather than reporting that enforcement was experienced.

evidence.quote: Who do you think sent us to do this interview?

claims.text: Respondent's attribution of who commissioned the survey, a perception with enumerated sponsor categories plus God and Other that need not match the actual commissioning body, so a mistaken attribution remains fully possible.

evidence.quote: Willing to participate in follow-up surveys

claims.text: Records stated willingness to be recontacted, with a separate not-applicable category for respondents lacking a mobile number, so absence of consent is not the same as refusal and willingness need not predict later participation.

inquiries.question: Do respondents who insist the president must obey law and courts also reject military intervention when elected leaders abuse power, or does the lawful-limits norm attach only to the elected executive?
inquiries.alternatives: Configuration A: firm anti-exemption paired with firm anti-intervention, a single lawful-process norm. Configuration B: firm anti-exemption paired with accepting takeover on abuse grounds, showing the norm is actor-specific. Configuration C: neither-agree responses showing the forced choice captures no committed position.
inquiries.ceiling: Depends on country and constitution resolving the bracketed office names, and takes expressed stances as evidence of stated norms only; no claim that either attitude predicts actual constitutional behaviour.

inquiries.question: Does a demand that government do more on women's equality travel with anticipated community harassment of a woman candidate or with a specific priority issue, and can the two diverge?
inquiries.alternatives: Configuration A: high harassment likelihood plus a more-action demand, coupling a perceived social barrier with a state remedy. Configuration B: high harassment likelihood but about-right effort, implying the barrier is seen as communal rather than governmental. Configuration C: low harassment likelihood with a priority choice, separating perceived climate from issue salience.
inquiries.ceiling: Requires documentation that all three gender items were asked of the same eligible respondents and that Q51B was not conditioned on a prior answer; establishes response-act configurations only, not whether harassment occurred and not the effect of government action.

inquiries.question: Do respondents who attribute the survey to a party or government differ in follow-up willingness from those naming a research or international body, and does the no-mobile route confound the comparison?
inquiries.alternatives: Configuration A: party-or-government attribution with declining follow-up, implying suspicion of the sponsor. Configuration B: research-body attribution with accepting follow-up, implying trust in an academic sponsor. Counterexample C: not-applicable cases concentrated among a sponsor group, making apparent refusal a coverage artifact.
inquiries.ceiling: Depends on qualifying the not-applicable route before reading willingness; establishes attributed sponsorship and stated willingness only, not true sponsor identity and not later participation, with no causal claim about trust.
